slides.title: File Concept
slides.body: File Concept
slides.notes: First of all we'll be learning about the File Concept

slides.title: Why Files Exist?
slides.body:
Persistent Data Storage
Process memory is volatile and disappears once execution ends. Operating systems provide files as a persistent, named abstraction for data on secondary storage
slides.notes: Now, this diagram shows what happens to data across the life of a process. When the process ends, its memory disappears, but the operating system can store the data as files in the file system, where it remains available on secondary storage. So, files provide the persistence that process memory cannot.

slides.title: Why Files Exist?
slides.body:
Persistent Data Storage
Process memory is reclaimed on exit; RAM clears on reboot
01
02
03
Files store data permanently on disk, SSD or tape
OS provides a uniform logical view over raw storage
04
File management is a core OS function
slides.notes: Moving on, process memory is temporary, so it is reclaimed when a process exits, and RAM is also cleared when the system reboots. Files provide long-term storage on devices such as disks, SSDs, or tapes. The OS hides the hardware-level storage details and gives users a consistent logical way to manage data, making file management a core OS responsibility.

slides.title: File Definition
slides.body:
Named Logical Unit
A file is a named collection of related information recorded on secondary storage. It is the smallest logical storage unit the operating system exposes
slides.notes: Next, think of a file as a single logical container that groups related data under a name. The OS treats this named unit as the basic way users and applications organize and access information on secondary storage.

slides.title: File Definition
slides.body:
Logical view: sequence of bytes, records or fields
01
02
03
Physical storage details are hidden by the file system
Structure and meaning are defined by the creating application
04
Files persist independent of the process that created them
Named Logical Unit
slides.notes: Now, from the OS perspective, a file can be viewed simply as a sequence of bytes, records, or fields, depending on how the data is organized. The file system hides where and how those contents are physically stored, while the application that creates the file determines its structure and meaning. Most importantly, the file continues to exist even after the creating process ends.

slides.title: File Definition
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Analogy: A school report card is a single named record holding a student's marks, attendance and remarks together exactly as a file bundles related data under one name for the operating system to manage.

slides.title: File
slides.body: Attributes

Type - Needed for systems supporting multiple file types
Location - Pointer to device and disk addressSize - Current file size in bytes
Protection - Access-control information for owner, group, others
Time & Date - Creation, last modification, last access stamps
User identification - Owner and, in some systems, creator ID

slides.title: File Operations
slides.body:
Create, Open, Read, Write
The operating system supports a defined set of operations on files, each implemented through a system call
slides.notes:
Moving on, files are managed through specific operations that let a process interact with stored data.
 Actions such as creating or opening a file establish access, while reading and writing allow the process to retrieve or modify its contents. The OS provides these operations through system calls.

slides.body: Create Open Read Write

slides.title: Open File Table
slides.body:
Tracking Active Files
Opening a file creates entries in the open-file tables so the operating system can track its state and access efficiently
slides.notes: Next, when a process opens a file, the OS needs to remember that the file is currently in use and how it is being accessed. It keeps this information in an open-file table, allowing later operations to track the file efficiently instead of starting from scratch each time.

slides.title: Open File Table
slides.body:
Per-process table stores the file pointer and access mode
System-wide table stores file metadata, disk location, and open count
File pointer marks the current read/write position
Multiple processes or file descriptors can reference the same system-wide entry
When the last reference is closed, the system can release the system-wide open-file entry
Tracking Active Files
slides.notes: Now, think of the open-file tables as the OS's way of remembering everything it needs about files currently in use. Each process keeps its own access information, such as where it is currently reading or writing, while the system-wide table keeps information shared by everyone accessing that file. This also allows multiple processes to safely refer to the same file, and once nobody is using it anymore, the OS can remove that shared entry.

slides.title: File Access Methods
slides.body: File Access Methods
slides.notes: Next we will learn about the File Access Methods

slides.title: Why Access Methods
slides.body:
Retrieval Pattern Choice
Different applications need different patterns to retrieve file data efficiently; the operating system offers distinct access methods matching each need
slides.notes: Moving on, not every application needs to retrieve data in the same way. For example, some applications process data from beginning to end, while others need to jump directly to a specific location. That is why the OS provides different file access methods, allowing applications to choose the pattern that best fits their needs.

slides.title: Why Access Methods
slides.body:
Retrieval Pattern Choice
Log files are read strictly in order, start to end
01
02
03
Databases need quick access to one specific record
Access method determines allowed operations and performance
04
05
Choice depends on storage device and usage pattern
Three main access methods exist: Sequential, Direct, and Indexed
slides.notes: Next, the way data is used determines which access method makes sense. A log file is naturally processed from start to end, while a database may need to jump directly to a particular record. So, the access method affects both what operations are possible and how efficiently they run, depending on the storage device and usage pattern. The three main methods are Sequential, Direct, and Indexed access.

slides.title: Sequential Access
slides.body:
Read In Order
Operations: read_next() and write_next() advance pointer automatically
01
02
03
reset() operation moves pointer back to file start
Optional skip of n records forward or backward
04
05
Natural fit for magnetic tape and log files
Simple to implement, needs minimal extra metadata >
slides.notes:
Sequential access reads or writes file records one after another from the beginning, matching how early storage media like tape operated
Moving on, sequential access is like going through a file from beginning to end, one record after another. 
The pointer automatically moves forward with each read or write, while reset() brings it back to the start. We can also skip records when needed. This makes the method simple and well suited for log files and magnetic tape, without requiring much extra metadata.

slides.body:

Sequential Access Method
slides.notes: Now, this diagram shows the basic flow of sequential access. The file is processed from the beginning toward the end, moving through Block-1, Block-2, Block-3, and so on in order. So, to reach Block-5, the system passes through the earlier blocks first rather than jumping directly to it.

slides.title: Direct Access (Relative Access)
slides.body:
File is viewed as a sequence of fixed-size blocks
01
02
03
Program supplies a relative block number to the OS
OS translates relative block number into absolute disk address
04
05
No need to read preceding blocks first
Requires a random-access device such as disk, not tape
06
Essential for database and relational record files
Jump To Block
slides.notes: Next, direct access is useful when the application already knows which block it needs. The file is divided into fixed-size blocks, and the program gives the OS a relative block number. The OS maps that number to the actual disk location, allowing it to jump directly to the required block without reading everything before it. That is why this method works well with random-access disks and is commonly used for databases and relational records.

slides.body:

Direct Access Method

slides.notes: Moving on, this diagram shows why direct access is called “jump to block.” The current position is at Block-2, but the system can directly move to Block-5 by specifying the required relative block number. It does not have to process Block-3 and Block-4 first, which makes random access much faster for applications that need specific records.

slides.title: Indexed Access
slides.body:
Index Locates Record
Index file holds pointers to actual data blocks
01
02
03
Looking up a key gives the block address instantly
Supports fast key-based search on very large files
04
05
Multiple indices possible, one per searchable key field
A very large index may itself need its own index
slides.notes: Now, indexed access works like a lookup system: instead of searching the entire file, the OS first checks an index that contains pointers to the actual data blocks. Once the required key is found, the corresponding block can be accessed directly, making searches much faster for large files. A file can have multiple indexes for different searchable fields, and if an index becomes very large, it may need another index to locate entries within it efficiently.

slides.title: Indexed Sequential Method
slides.body:
ISAM Combines Both
Indexed Sequential Access Method (ISAM) combines sequential and indexed access, using a small master index to jump to a block, then scanning sequentially within it
slides.notes: Moving on, ISAM combines the strengths of both approaches. The master index first helps us jump close to the required block, and then the records within that block are read sequentially. So, we get faster locating than pure sequential access while still benefiting from ordered scanning.

slides.title: Indexed Sequential Method
slides.body:
ISAM Combines Both
Master index holds one entry per group of records
01
02
03
Index lookup narrows search to a small block range
Sequential scan inside that block finds the exact record
04
05
Reduces index size versus indexing every single record
Classic scheme used in early database and file systems
slides.notes: Next, think of ISAM as a two-step search. The master index keeps one entry for each group of records, so it quickly narrows the search to a small block range. We then scan that group sequentially to find the exact record. This avoids indexing every record individually, keeping the index smaller, and was a classic approach in early database and file systems.

slides.title: Indexed Sequential Method
slides.body:
ISAM Combines Both
Index Access Method
slides.notes: Now, this diagram shows how the index acts as a shortcut to the data. The index file points to a location in secondary storage, and from that point, the related records can be reached rather than searching through the entire file. So, ISAM first uses the index to narrow down the location and then works with the records in that area.

slides.title: Directory Structure
slides.body: Directory Structure
slides.notes: Next we will learn about the Directory structure

slides.title: Why Directories Needed
slides.body:
A directory is a special file that maps file names to their storage locations, letting the operating system organise many files logically
Organizing Many Files
slides.notes: Moving on, as the number of files grows, keeping track of each file individually becomes difficult. A directory solves this by maintaining the names and their corresponding storage information, giving the OS a structured way to organize and locate files.

slides.title: Why Directories Needed
slides.body:
Thousands of files without grouping become impossible to locate
01
02
03
Directory maps human-readable names to file locations on disk
Directories let files be organised into logical groups
04
05
Structure choice balances usability against search efficiency
Five common structures: Single-Level, Two-Level, Tree, Acyclic-Graph, General-Graph
Organizing Many Files
slides.notes: So, once a system has a large number of files, the real challenge is not storing them but finding and managing them efficiently. Directories give us that organization by grouping related files and connecting their names with where the files are stored. Depending on how much organization and search efficiency we need, the OS supports five directory structures: Single-Level, Two-Level, Tree, Acyclic-Graph, and General-Graph.

slides.title: Directory Operations
slides.body:
Core Four Operations
Every directory implementation supports a defined set of operations for managing the entries it contains
tables: Add a new file or subdirectory entry
Locate an entry by name for access
Remove an entry and free its space
Enumerate all entries in a directory

slides.title: Single-Level Directory
slides.body:
One Flat List
In a single-level directory, every file for every user is listed in one common directory without subdirectories at all, with every file needing a unique name
slides.notes: Moving on, the simplest approach is to keep every user's file in one common directory. The diagram shows this flat structure, where D1 through D8 each point directly to a file, with no subdirectories. The limitation is that every file must have a unique name, which becomes difficult to manage as the number of files grows.

slides.title: Single-Level Directory
slides.body:
One Flat List
01
Simplest structure to implement and understand
02
03
Name collisions between different users are a major limitation
Impractical once file count or user count grows
slides.notes: Now, the advantage of this structure is its simplicity—it is easy to create and understand. But because everyone shares the same directory, two users cannot have files with the same name. As the number of users and files increases, managing this flat list quickly becomes impractical.

slides.title: Two-Level Directory
slides.body:
Per-User Directories
A two-level directory gives each user their own User File Directory (UFD) listed under one Master File Directory (MFD), solving name collisions
slides.notes: Moving on, the two-level structure separates users instead of putting everyone's files together. The Master File Directory acts as the top level and points to a separate User File Directory for each user. In the diagram, each user directory can contain files with the same name without conflict, which solves the major naming problem of a single-level directory.

slides.title: Two-Level Directory
slides.body:
Per-User Directories
01
Same file name is now allowed across different users
02
03
Searching within one user's files is still unstructured
Sharing files across users remains difficult or impossible
slides.notes: Now, separating files by user solves the naming conflict, so different users can have files with the same name. But inside each user's directory, there is still no deeper organization, making large collections harder to search. Also, because each user has a separate directory, sharing files between users is not straightforward.

slides.title: Tree Directory
slides.body:
Hierarchical Subdirectories
A tree-structured directory generalises the two-level scheme, letting users create subdirectories to any depth under a single root
slides.notes: Next, the tree structure takes the idea of separate user directories one step further by allowing subdirectories within them, to any depth. In the diagram, the root directory branches into user directories, which can contain both files and further subdirectories like Sd1 and Sd2. This hierarchical organization makes large collections much easier to manage and locate.

slides.title: Tree Directory
slides.body:
Hierarchical Subdirectories
01
Every file has one unique absolute path from root
02
03
Current working directory enables shorter relative paths
Most widely used structure in modern operating systems
slides.notes: Moving on, the tree structure gives each file a clear location within the hierarchy, so we can identify it using a unique absolute path starting from the root. For everyday navigation, the current working directory lets us use shorter relative paths. This flexibility is why the tree structure is the standard approach in most modern operating systems.

slides.title: Acyclic Graph Directory
slides.body:
Shared Subdirectories Links
An acyclic-graph directory extends the tree by allowing a file or subdirectory to be shared between directories through links, while forbidding cycles
D1
D11
D12
D13
Root
Directory
User
Directory
Files and Subdirectories
Sd1
Sd2
slides.notes:
Now, an acyclic-graph directory extends the tree by allowing the same file or subdirectory to be shared through links.
 In the diagram, multiple directories can point to the same item, so users can access shared data without creating duplicate copies. The important restriction is that these links cannot form a cycle, keeping the directory structure acyclic.

slides.title: Acyclic Graph Directory
slides.body:
Shared Subdirectories Links
01
02
Sharing is implemented through links or shared directory entries
Structure must stay acyclic to keep traversal and deletion safe
03
04
Deleting a shared file needs reference counting or link checks
Trades some structural complexity for genuine file sharing
slides.notes: Next, this structure allows genuine sharing by letting multiple directories point to the same file or subdirectory through links. The OS must prevent those links from forming a cycle, otherwise traversal and deletion become difficult to manage. When a shared file is deleted, the OS therefore needs to check whether other links still reference it, typically using reference counting. So, we gain file sharing at the cost of some additional structural complexity.

slides.title: General Graph Directory
slides.body:
Cycles Allowed
A general graph directory permits arbitrary links between directories, including links that loop back and form a cycle, unlike the acyclic-graph structure, which explicitly forbids this
slides.notes: Finally, a general-graph directory allows arbitrary links between directories, even when those links create cycles. In the diagram, the Root Directory branches to User-1, User-2, and User-3. User-1 contains File-1, while User-3 contains File-2. User-2 connects to the Subdirectory, and the subdirectory has a link back toward User-2, creating a cycle. So, unlike an acyclic graph, the same directory can be reached again by following links. This gives greater flexibility for sharing and organization, but makes traversal, searching, and deletion more difficult because the OS has to handle these cycles safely.

slides.title: General Graph Directory
slides.body:
Cycles Allowed
01
Simple reference counting cannot reclaim cyclic directories
02
03
Requires cycle detection or garbage collection to reclaim unreachable space
Traversal algorithms must track already-visited directories to avoid looping forever
slides.notes: Now, allowing cycles creates an important problem for the OS. With a cyclic structure, reference counting alone may not free a directory, because objects in the cycle can continue to reference one another even when nothing outside the cycle can reach them. So, the OS needs cycle detection or garbage collection to reclaim such unreachable space. Also, while traversing directories, it must remember which directories it has already visited; otherwise, it could keep following the cycle forever.

slides.title: Why Layers Exist
slides.body:
Separating Storage Concerns
Each layer handles one well-defined responsibility only
01
02
03
Lower layers hide device-specific details from upper layers
A layer can be modified or replaced with minimal impact on other layers
04
Matches the layered design philosophy seen in OS structure
slides.notes: Moving on, the idea of layering is to keep storage management from becoming one large, complicated task. Each layer takes care of a specific responsibility and hides its implementation details from the layer above it. This separation means one layer can be changed or replaced with minimal effect on the others, following the same layered design philosophy used throughout operating systems.

slides.title: File System Layers
slides.body:
Application To Devices
Application Programs
Logical File System
File organization module
Basic file system
I/O Control
Devices
slides.notes: Moving on, this diagram shows how a file request travels through the system, from the application down to the actual storage device. The Application Program starts the request, which passes through the Logical File System, File Organization Module, and Basic File System. Then I/O Control handles the device-specific communication before reaching the Devices layer. Each layer performs its own responsibility and passes the request downward, while hiding its implementation details from the layer above.

slides.title: File System Architecture
slides.body: File System Architecture
slides.notes: Now we will learn about the File system Architecture

slides.title: On-Disk Structures
slides.body:
Boot Block Superblock FCB
Persistent metadata is itself stored on disk alongside file data, so the file system can rebuild its state after every reboot
slides.notes: Now, the file system also needs to preserve its own information on disk, so it can reconstruct its state after a reboot. The boot block contains information needed to start the OS, while the superblock keeps volume-level details such as block size and free-space information. The directory structure connects file names with the volume, and the File Control Block, commonly represented by an inode, stores details specific to each file, such as its size, permissions, and block locations.
tables: Info needed to boot OS from that volume
Free block count, block size, free-block pointers
Organises file names into the volume
Per-file details — permissions, size, block locations

slides.title: In-Memory Structures
slides.body:
Mount And Open Tables
Alongside on-disk metadata, the operating system keeps in-memory structures during runtime to avoid repeated disk reads for active files
slides.notes: Moving on, unlike the metadata stored permanently on disk, these structures stay in memory while the system is running to make file access faster. The mount table tracks mounted file systems, while the directory cache keeps recently used directory information. For open files, the OS maintains both system-wide and per-process tables, and the buffer or disk cache keeps recently accessed blocks ready in memory, reducing repeated disk access.
tables: Tracks each mounted file system and its mount point
Recently accessed directory information kept in memory
One entry per open file, holds a copy of its FCB
Pointer from process file descriptor into system-wide table
Recently read or written blocks held in memory

slides.title: Partitions And Volumes
slides.body:
Raw Vs Cooked
A physical disk is divided into partitions, and one or more partitions form a volume that either holds a file system or stays raw
slides.notes: Now, a physical disk can be divided into separate partitions, which provide independent regions of storage. These partitions can then be combined to form a volume. A volume may be cooked, meaning it contains a file system and can store files normally, or raw, meaning it is available directly to an application without a file system managing its contents.

slides.title: Partitions And Volumes
slides.body:
Raw Vs Cooked
Raw partition holds no file system, used for swap space or database raw storage
01
02
03
Cooked partition contains a formatted file system ready for normal files
Root partition holds the OS kernel and is mounted first at boot
04
05
A volume can span multiple storage devices or partitions
Boot information is often kept in its own small boot partition
slides.notes: Moving on, the key difference is whether the storage has a file system on it. A raw partition has no file system and can be used for things like swap space or specialized database storage, while a cooked partition is formatted and ready for normal files. During boot, the root partition provides the OS kernel and is mounted early, while boot information may be kept separately in a small boot partition. Also, a volume is not necessarily limited to one physical partition—it can span multiple storage devices or partitions.

slides.title: Virtual File System
slides.body:
Uniform Access Layer
The Virtual File System (VFS) is a kernel abstraction layer giving one uniform API over multiple, possibly different, underlying file system types
slides.notes: So, applications should not need to know which specific file system is managing their data. The VFS acts as a common interface between applications and different file-system implementations, so the same file operations can work across multiple file-system types without changing the application.

slides.title: Virtual File System
slides.body:
Uniform Access Layer
Open, read, write, and close work across file systems, with VFS providing a common interface for local and remote Systems
01
02
03
New file system types can be added without changing application code
Implemented as an object-oriented interface inside the kernel
slides.notes: Next, think of VFS as the common layer that hides the differences between file systems. Applications can use operations like open, read, write, and close without knowing which file system is underneath, whether it is local or remote. This also means a new file system can be added without changing application code, while the kernel provides this through an object-oriented interface.

slides.title: Mounting A Filesystem
slides.body:
Attaching At Mount Point
A file system must be mounted, attached at a specific mount point in the existing directory tree, before any of its files become accessible
slides.notes: Now, think of mounting as attaching one file system to a location that already exists in the directory tree. In the diagram, the file system on the left is mounted onto the highlighted mount point in the existing tree. Once attached, the files and directories inside that file system become accessible through that location; before mounting, they cannot be accessed through the directory tree.

slides.title: Mounting A Filesystem
slides.body:
Attaching At Mount Point
01
02
The OS verifies that the device contains a valid, recognizablefile system
The root file system mounts automatically at boot; other volumes mount at boot or later manually
03
New entry records the device and its mount point
slides.notes: Moving on, before the OS attaches a storage device to the directory tree, it first makes sure the device is usable as a file system. The root file system is needed during startup, so it is mounted as part of the boot process, while additional volumes can be connected later when required. Once the attachment is established, the OS remembers which device is connected where, so file access can be routed correctly.

slides.title: Types Of Access
slides.body: Six Access Rights
slides.notes: Operating systems define specific access rights rather than one all-or-nothing permission, letting owners grant exactly the operations a user needs
tables: Add data only at file end
View file name in directory listing

slides.title: Protection
slides.body: Protection
slides.notes: Next we will understand about the Protection

slides.title: Why Protection Needed
slides.body:
Multi-User Access Risk
Uncontrolled access risks accidental or malicious data loss
01
02
03
Sensitive files need restricted read or write rights
Protection extends the sharing already enabled by directories
04
Operating system enforces the rules set by the file owner
slides.notes: So, once files are shared through directories, the OS also needs to control who can actually use them. Without protection, one user or process could accidentally or intentionally modify another user's data. The file owner defines the required access rights, and the operating system enforces those rules for users and processes.

slides.title: Why Protection Needed
slides.body:
Systems either attach a detailed access-control list to each file or classify users into broad groups to keep permission storage compact
Multi-User Access Risk
slides.notes: Now, the OS needs an efficient way to store these access rules. It can maintain a detailed access-control list when different users need different permissions, or use broader user groups when many users share the same access requirements. This balances fine-grained control with efficient permission storage.

slides.title: Unix Permission Bits
slides.body:
Owner, Group, Other
Traditional Unix packs read, write and execute rights for owner, group and other into nine bits, shown as rwx triplets in a directory listing
slides.notes:
Moving on, Unix keeps permissions compact by dividing users into three categories: owner, group, and other. 
Each category gets three possible rights—read, write, and execute—which together form the familiar nine-bit rwx permission pattern.

slides.title: Special Permission Bits
slides.body:
Setuid, Setgid, Sticky
Beyond the standard nine bits, Unix defines three special permission bits that change how execution and directory deletion behave
slides.notes: Next, Unix also has three special permission bits that go beyond the normal rwx permissions. Setuid and setgid affect the identity under which a program executes, while the sticky bit controls who can delete entries in a shared directory.
